newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan dismisses U.S. nuclear objections.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan dismisses U.S. nuclear objections.

text.p: Pakistan on Tuesday dismissed the latest U.S. objection to what it calls its peaceful nuclear cooperation with China, saying this did not violate any international convention or law.
The United States urged China on Monday to halt all nuclear cooperation with Pakistan despite assurances by Beijing that it had not given nuclear technology for military purposes.

Asked to comment on the statement, a Pakistan Foreign Ministry spokesman told Reuters that Sino-Pakistan cooperation for the use of nuclear energy came under International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards and any country had the right to engage in such cooperation.
"No international convention or law has been violated," he said. "No country should object to this."

An official accompanying Chinese President Jiang Zemin on a visit to Pakistan said on Sunday that Beijing would continue its cooperation with Islamabad "in the utilisation of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes".

A U.S. State Department spokesman said it was long-standing U.S. policy "that the United States does not participate in or encourage in any way any kind of nuclear trade or nuclear cooperation, even with safeguarded facilities, in Pakistan."
"We think that it's best that China refrain from any type of nuclear cooperation with Pakistan," spokesman Nicholas Burns told a news briefing in Washington.
"If the United States has objections, it is their opinion," the Pakistani spokesman said, adding: "There can be no objection to this (Pakistan-China cooperation) under international law."
Pakistan, like its rival India, has not signed the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and is considered by the United States a "threshold" nuclear power that could quickly assemble a nuclear weapon.
Burns said he was not surprised by the Chinese statement "because, you know, we don't always see eye-to-eye with the Chinese on this particular issue".
Washington and Beijing held lengthy talks earlier this year on sales by a Chinese firm of ring magnets, which can be used in nuclear weapons production, to Pakistan.
Eventually U.S. officials accepted assurances by the Chinese government that it had not known of the sale. Beijing pledged in May that it would make no further such transfers.
Burns repeated previous U.S. assertions that Washington was not aware of any Chinese violations of that pledge, or of Chinese missile sales to Pakistan that would violate U.S. laws.

Contravention by Beijing of those laws through missile or nuclear technology sales -- both of which have been repeatedly alleged in U.S. press reports -- could entail the imposition of U.S. sanctions on China.
